meta.subject: PYTHON
meta.author: bank-team-python
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.learningObjective: Trace instance creation from a class definition
questions.stem: A transit planner writes class Route: pass then r = Route(). What does r.__class__ return?

options.text: The module object that holds the class definition
options.misconception: confuses the defining module with the class object

options.text: An instance of Route created at import time
None because pass leaves the class empty
options.misconception: assumes an empty body prevents class creation

questions.explanation: Instantiating Route calls the class and returns an object whose __class__ is Route. An empty body is still a valid class, and construction happens at call time.
questions.hint: Instantiating a class returns an instance of it.

questions.topic: One Attribute Held By The Class
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish class attributes from instance attributes
questions.stem: In a transit planner's Route class, color = 'blue' is set in the class body. Two Route instances are made. What is true?

options.text: Each instance gets its own separate copy of color
options.misconception: treats a class attribute as an instance attribute

options.text: color is deleted after the first instance is created
Both instances share the same color binding
color becomes a method because it lacks self
options.misconception: confuses attribute binding with method definition

questions.explanation: Attributes defined in the class body belong to the class and are shared by all instances until an instance rebinds its own. Nothing is consumed on instantiation.
questions.hint: Class body names are shared by default.

questions.topic: What A Double-Under Method Is For
questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of a dunder method
questions.stem: A transit planner asks what __init__ is for in a Stop class. Which answer is right?

options.text: It defines how instances are compared for equality
It runs when the class is subclassed by another
It returns the printable text of an instance
It initializes a newly created instance

questions.explanation: __init__ is the initializer called after instance creation to set up state. Comparison, subclassing, and text forms use other dunders.

questions.topic: Two Hooks Driving One Operation
questions.stem: A transit planner wonders why Python has both __new__ and __init__. Explain in one model answer.

answer.exemplar: __new__ creates and returns the instance before __init__ receives it to set up state, so creation and initialization stay separate concerns in Python classes.

questions.explanation: __new__ is the constructor that allocates the object, while __init__ only initializes it. Separating them lets immutable types and metaclasses control creation.

questions.topic: When The Construction Hook Runs
questions.stem: A transit planner defines class Trip with __init__. When does __init__ run?

options.text: When an instance is created by calling the class
When the class object itself is created at definition
options.misconception: confuses class creation with instance creation

options.text: When a subclass overrides a method

questions.explanation: Calling the class triggers __new__ then __init__. Class definition, overriding, and import do not call __init__.
questions.hint: Calling the class builds an instance.

questions.topic: The Two Text Forms Of An Object
questions.stem: A transit planner asks which two dunders define an object's text forms. Which pair?
questions.explanation: __str__ gives the readable form and __repr__ gives the developer form. __format__ and __bytes__ serve other purposes.

questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.learningObjective: Match str and repr to audiences
questions.stem: A transit planner prints an object in a user report versus a debugger. Which form suits each?

options.text: Both forms are identical in every case
options.misconception: assumes str and repr never differ

options.text: Neither form is ever shown to users

questions.explanation: __str__ targets end users with readable text, while __repr__ targets developers with unambiguous detail. They often differ.
questions.hint: Users read str, developers read repr.

questions.topic: Equality And Hashing That Disagree
questions.stem: A transit planner defines __eq__ on Stop but leaves __hash__ as None. What breaks?

options.text: Stop instances can no longer be compared with ==

options.misconception: limits the impact to mutable attributes

options.text: Hashing speed improves because None skips work
Stop instances become unhashable and unusable in sets

questions.explanation: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable. They cannot be used in sets or as dict keys.
questions.hint: Custom equality removes hashing by default.

questions.topic: A Method The Subclass Replaces
questions.stem: A transit planner subclasses ExpressRoute from Route and redefines fare(). Which method runs on ExpressRoute()?

options.text: ExpressRoute.fare because the subclass replaces it
Route.fare because the subclass inherits unchanged
options.misconception: ignores the override in the subclass

options.text: Neither runs because fare is not called explicitly

questions.explanation: A subclass method with the same name overrides the parent method. Calling fare on an instance uses the subclass version.

questions.topic: Reaching The Parent Explicitly
questions.learningObjective: Use super to call a parent method
questions.stem: A transit planner writes super().__init__() inside ExpressRoute.__init__. What does it do?

options.text: Creates a new unrelated Route instance
options.misconception: treats super as a constructor call for a new object
assumes super changes the class identity

options.text: Calls Route.__init__ on the current instance

questions.explanation: super() returns a proxy to the parent class, so super().__init__() initializes the current instance using Route's logic.

questions.topic: Arranging Two Parents
questions.stem: A transit planner writes class MetroBus(Route, Vehicle). What is the parent order?

options.text: Only the first parent is kept
options.misconception: thinks multiple inheritance drops later parents

questions.explanation: Parents are listed left to right in the declaration. The MRO uses that order as a starting point.
questions.hint: Declaration order is left to right.

questions.topic: The Order A Search Walks
questions.stem: A transit planner asks what MRO stands for. Which expansion is correct?

options.misconception: confuses memory layout with lookup order

questions.explanation: MRO is Method Resolution Order, the linearized search path Python uses for attributes and methods.
questions.hint: It is the lookup path for methods.

questions.topic: A Value Computed On Every Read
questions.stem: A transit planner wraps distance with @property. What happens on each access?

options.text: The value is cached after the first read
Access raises an error without a setter
options.misconception: thinks setters are required for reads

options.text: The value is computed only at construction
The getter runs every time the attribute is read

questions.explanation: A property invokes its getter on every access, so the value is recomputed each time unless you cache manually.

questions.topic: A Value Shared Until An Object Sets Its Own
questions.learningObjective: Explain class attribute sharing and override
questions.stem: A transit planner sets a class attribute fare then assigns instance.fare = 5. Explain the result.

answer.exemplar: The instance now has its own fare attribute that shadows the class attribute, while other instances still see the shared class value.

questions.explanation: Instance assignment creates an instance attribute that shadows the class attribute. Other instances keep seeing the shared class value.
questions.hint: Instance assignment shadows the class value.

questions.topic: An Attribute That Arrives On Its Own
questions.stem: A transit planner defines __getattr__ on Route. When does it run?

options.text: On every attribute access including existing ones

options.misconception: limits it to class creation time

options.text: Only for private names starting with underscore

questions.explanation: __getattr__ is a fallback called only when normal attribute lookup fails. __getattribute__ runs on every access.

questions.topic: Catching A Parent Class
questions.learningObjective: Use except with a base exception
questions.stem: A transit planner writes except Exception as e. Which errors does it catch?

options.text: Only errors raised in the try block

questions.explanation: An except clause catches the named exception and all its subclasses. BaseException is broader and includes SystemExit.

questions.topic: A Fault That Carries Its Own Numbers
questions.learningObjective: Store data in a custom exception
questions.stem: A transit planner raises DelayError(minutes=12). Where can minutes be read?

options.misconception: thinks data lives only in traceback

options.text: It cannot be read after raising

questions.explanation: A custom exception can store data as instance attributes accessible after catching. Tracebacks and docstrings are not the channel.

questions.topic: A Hand-Written Context Manager
questions.stem: A transit planner writes a class with __enter__ and __exit__. What protocol is it?
questions.explanation: __enter__ and __exit__ implement the context manager protocol used by with statements.

questions.topic: One Check Over Several Cases
questions.learningObjective: Use parametrize to run multiple cases
questions.stem: A transit planner uses pytest.mark.parametrize. What does it produce?

options.text: A single test run with all cases combined
options.misconception: thinks cases collapse into one run

options.text: A skipped test for each case
Multiple test invocations from one function

questions.explanation: parametrize generates one test invocation per parameter set, reported separately. It is not skipping or fixture sharing.

questions.topic: One Assertion Over Several Cases
questions.stem: A transit planner wraps code in pytest.raises(ValueError). What is checked?
questions.explanation: pytest.raises asserts that the block raises the named exception. It fails if no exception or a different one occurs.

questions.topic: A Method That Needs Neither Self Nor The Class
questions.stem: A transit planner has a helper that uses no instance or class state. Which decorator fits?

options.misconception: uses classmethod when no class state is needed

questions.explanation: staticmethod defines a function with no implicit self or cls. classmethod, property, and abstractmethod serve different purposes.

questions.topic: Shared Setup That Survives Between Tests
questions.stem: A transit planner defines a pytest fixture with no scope argument. What is its scope?
questions.explanation: The default fixture scope is function, so setup runs once per test function. Other scopes must be requested explicitly.

questions.topic: What A Setup Can Be Narrowed To
questions.stem: A transit planner asks why choose session scope for a database fixture. Explain briefly.

answer.exemplar: Session scope builds the database once for the whole run, saving setup cost when tests only read shared state.

questions.explanation: A broader scope reduces repeated setup cost but risks shared mutable state. Choose scope based on isolation needs.

questions.topic: Standing In For A Collaborator
questions.stem: A transit planner replaces a network client with a fake in a test. What is this called?

options.misconception: confuses test double with code restructuring
confuses test double with static analysis
confuses test double with performance measurement

questions.explanation: Replacing a collaborator with a controlled fake is mocking. Refactoring, linting, and profiling are unrelated activities.

questions.topic: Two Calls Recorded And Counted
questions.stem: A transit planner mocks a client and calls send twice. How many calls does mock.send.call_count equal?
questions.explanation: Each call increments call_count, so two calls yield 2. The count reflects invocations, not arguments.

questions.topic: Why Equality And Hashing Must Agree
questions.stem: A transit planner asks why equal objects must have equal hashes. Explain briefly.

answer.exemplar: If two objects compare equal but hash differently, a set or dict may store both and break lookup invariants.

questions.explanation: The contract requires equal objects to share a hash so sets and dicts can find them. Violating it causes duplicate storage and failed lookups.

questions.topic: An Assertion That Stops The Test
questions.stem: A transit planner writes assert x == 5 in a test. What happens if x is 3?

options.text: A warning is logged and test continues

questions.explanation: A failed assert raises AssertionError and stops the test. It does not skip, correct, or warn.

questions.topic: An Assertion That Checks Almost Nothing
questions.stem: A transit planner's test ends with assert result is not None. Why is this weak?

options.text: It passes for almost any non-None value
It raises an error on booleans

questions.explanation: assert result is not None passes for many wrong values, so it checks almost nothing. A stronger assertion compares the expected value.

questions.topic: A Total Over No Values
questions.stem: A transit planner calls sum([]) for an empty list of delays. What is the result?
questions.explanation: sum of an empty iterable is 0, the default start. No items contribute to the total.

questions.topic: A Default That Was Never Replaced
questions.stem: A transit planner uses def add_stop(stops=[]). What is the pitfall?

options.text: The list is recreated each call
The same list is shared across calls

questions.explanation: A mutable default is evaluated once at definition time, so the same list persists across calls and accumulates state.

questions.topic: What A Setup Scope Decides
questions.stem: A transit planner changes a fixture scope from function to module. What changes?

options.text: The fixture runs after every test
Only one test can use it
The fixture value is cached across tests in the module

questions.explanation: Module scope runs setup once per module and reuses the value across tests in that module. It does not restrict usage or parametrize.

questions.topic: A Row Shorter Than The Header
questions.learningObjective: Handle short rows in CSV reading
questions.stem: A transit planner reads CSV rows and one row has fewer fields than the header. What is likely?

options.text: The reader raises an error automatically
options.misconception: assumes automatic error on short rows
thinks header adapts to row length

options.text: Missing fields are filled with None or empty

questions.explanation: CSV readers typically pad short rows with None or empty strings rather than raising or skipping. Check your reader's behavior.

questions.topic: Comparing Two Kinds Of Instant
questions.learningObjective: Compare datetime with and without tzinfo
questions.stem: A transit planner compares a naive datetime with an aware one. What happens?

options.text: They compare equal if wall times match
The aware one loses its tzinfo
The naive one is treated as UTC

questions.explanation: Comparing naive and aware datetimes raises TypeError because Python cannot reconcile the missing timezone.

questions.topic: Records Filed Under A Key
questions.stem: A transit planner uses defaultdict(list) and accesses a missing key. What happens?

options.text: An empty list is created and returned

questions.explanation: defaultdict calls the factory for missing keys, so accessing a missing key creates and returns an empty list.

questions.topic: What A Declaration Writes For You
questions.stem: A transit planner decorates a class with @dataclass. What is generated?
questions.explanation: @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by default, with options to add more. It does not create tables.

questions.topic: A Fault That Names The Family
questions.stem: A transit planner defines class DelayError(TransitError). What relationship exists?

options.text: They are aliases of the same class

questions.explanation: Declaring DelayError(TransitError) makes DelayError a subclass, so catching TransitError also catches DelayError.

questions.topic: The Three Parts Of A Test
questions.stem: A transit planner structures a test as setup, call, check. What is this pattern?
questions.explanation: Arrange-Act-Assert names the three phases: set up, invoke, verify. Given-When-Then is the BDD equivalent.

questions.topic: How Many Calls One Request Made
questions.learningObjective: Count calls recorded by a mock
questions.stem: A transit planner's mock records 3 calls to fetch and 2 calls to save. How many total calls?
questions.explanation: Add the recorded calls: 3 plus 2 equals 5. The total reflects distinct invocations.

questions.topic: A Total Built From A Table Of Records
questions.stem: A transit planner sums fares [2,3,4,5] for four riders. What is the total fare?
questions.explanation: 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 14. Sum each record's fare once.

questions.topic: Reaching The Class And Not The Object
questions.stem: A transit planner accesses obj.__class__. What does it return?

options.text: The class that created the instance

questions.explanation: __class__ points to the class that created the instance. __dict__ holds instance attributes, not the class.

questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.learningObjective: Trace instance creation from a class definition
questions.stem: A transit planner writes class Stop: pass. First, is Stop callable? Second, what does Stop() return?
questions.explanation: Classes are callable and calling one creates an instance. pass does not prevent instantiation.

questions.topic: One Attribute Held By The Class
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish class attributes from instance attributes
questions.stem: A transit planner changes a class attribute on one instance. Do other instances see the change?

options.text: Yes, all instances share the new value
options.misconception: thinks instance change propagates to class

options.text: No, and the instance change is ignored

questions.explanation: Assigning on an instance creates an instance attribute that shadows the class value; other instances keep the original.

questions.topic: What A Double-Under Method Is For
questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of a dunder method
questions.stem: A transit planner asks what __len__ is for. Which answer is right?

options.text: It converts an object to an integer index
It returns the memory size in bytes
It returns the number of items
It checks whether the object is empty

questions.explanation: __len__ returns the number of items so len() works. It is not about conversion, memory, or truthiness.

questions.topic: Two Hooks Driving One Operation
questions.stem: A transit planner asks which hook can return a different class instance. Which one?
questions.explanation: __new__ creates and can return an instance of a different class. __init__ only initializes the already created object.

questions.topic: When The Construction Hook Runs
questions.stem: A transit planner calls Route() inside a loop of 3 iterations. How many times does __init__ run?
questions.explanation: Each call to Route() runs __init__ once, so 3 iterations yield 3 runs.

questions.topic: The Two Text Forms Of An Object
questions.stem: A transit planner asks which function uses __repr__ by default. Which one?
questions.explanation: repr() uses __repr__, while str() and print() use __str__. input() reads text and is unrelated.

questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.learningObjective: Match str and repr to audiences
questions.stem: A transit planner wants an unambiguous developer string. Which dunder should they implement carefully?
questions.explanation: __repr__ should be unambiguous and ideally eval-able. __str__ is for readable user output.

questions.topic: Equality And Hashing That Disagree
questions.stem: A transit planner defines __eq__ and wants instances hashable. What must they do?
questions.explanation: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, so you must implement __hash__ explicitly to keep instances hashable.

questions.topic: A Method The Subclass Replaces
questions.stem: A transit planner calls super().fare() inside an override. What does it do?

options.text: Runs the parent version on the same instance

options.misconception: thinks super replaces rather than delegates
assumes super is invalid in methods

questions.explanation: super().fare() delegates to the parent implementation on the current instance, allowing reuse of parent logic.

questions.topic: Reaching The Parent Explicitly
questions.learningObjective: Use super to call a parent method
questions.stem: A transit planner writes Route.__init__(self). Is this equivalent to super().__init__()?
questions.explanation: Explicit parent calls bypass the MRO and can break cooperative multiple inheritance. super() follows the MRO.

questions.topic: Arranging Two Parents
questions.stem: A transit planner asks whether Python supports multiple inheritance. Is it supported?

options.text: Yes, but only for built-in types

questions.explanation: Python supports multiple inheritance by listing multiple base classes. It is not restricted to built-ins or mixins.

questions.topic: The Order A Search Walks
questions.stem: A transit planner wants to inspect the MRO of a class. Which attribute helps?

options.misconception: confuses direct bases with full MRO

questions.explanation: __mro__ is a tuple of classes in resolution order. __bases__ only lists direct parents.

questions.topic: A Value Computed On Every Read
questions.stem: A transit planner deletes a property's setter. What happens on assignment?
questions.explanation: A property without a setter raises AttributeError on assignment. There is no fallback storage or default setter.

questions.topic: A Value Shared Until An Object Sets Its Own
questions.learningObjective: Explain class attribute sharing and override
questions.stem: A transit planner mutates a shared list class attribute via one instance. Do other instances see the mutation?

options.text: No, each instance has its own list
Yes, but only after garbage collection
Yes, because the same list object is shared

questions.explanation: Mutating a shared mutable class attribute affects all instances because they reference the same object. Rebinding would shadow instead.

questions.topic: An Attribute That Arrives On Its Own
questions.stem: A transit planner asks whether __getattr__ is called for existing attributes. Is it?

options.text: No, and it is never called

questions.explanation: __getattr__ runs only when normal lookup fails, so existing attributes bypass it. __getattribute__ runs on every access.

questions.topic: Catching A Parent Class
questions.learningObjective: Use except with a base exception
questions.stem: A transit planner catches TransitError. Does it catch DelayError(TransitError)?

options.text: Yes, but only the first time

questions.explanation: An except clause catches subclasses, so TransitError catches DelayError. No re-raise or one-time rule applies.

questions.topic: A Fault That Carries Its Own Numbers
questions.learningObjective: Store data in a custom exception
questions.stem: A transit planner wants to attach a code to an exception. Best approach?

options.misconception: uses output instead of exception data

options.text: Put it in the class name
Store it as an instance attribute

questions.explanation: Storing data as an instance attribute keeps it accessible after catching. Printing or renaming does not.

questions.topic: A Hand-Written Context Manager
questions.stem: A transit planner's __exit__ returns True. What effect does that have?
questions.explanation: Returning True from __exit__ suppresses the exception. False or None lets it propagate.

questions.topic: One Check Over Several Cases
questions.learningObjective: Use parametrize to run multiple cases
questions.stem: A transit planner parametrizes a test with 4 cases. How many test results appear?
questions.explanation: parametrize produces one result per case, so 4 cases yield 4 results. They are not collapsed or doubled.

questions.topic: One Assertion Over Several Cases
questions.stem: A transit planner's pytest.raises block completes without raising. What is the test outcome?
questions.explanation: pytest.raises fails if the expected exception is not raised. It does not pass, skip, or error.
